p1_4_gamma_scan.description: Exploratory scan of how the average number of tokens produced per round (== per target-model forward pass) changes as gamma varies. Not a statistical hypothesis test like P1.3 -- a first characterization of the shape of the curve for this draft/target pair.
prompts: Write a Python function that checks whether a number is prime.
Explain why the sky is blue in simple terms.
Return a JSON object with fields name, age, and city.
p1_4_gamma_scan.sanity_check: max_round_length == gamma + 1 for every gamma tested (2,4,6,8,11), matching the theoretical per-round ceiling exactly -- no round ever produced more tokens than the algorithm allows, which is a basic correctness check the implementation passes.
p1_4_gamma_scan.headline_finding: Mean round length rises sharply from gamma=1 (1.697) to gamma=5 (3.980), then plateaus and slightly dips by gamma=10 (3.904) -- consistent with the expected diminishing-returns shape: larger gamma raises the theoretical per-round ceiling (gamma+1) but also lengthens the chain of candidates that must survive accept/reject in a row, so gains shrink and can reverse.
p1_4_gamma_scan.sample_size_caveat: Total rounds fall sharply as gamma grows (119 -> 67 -> 51 -> 52 -> 52) because each prompt has a fixed max_new_tokens=40 budget, and larger gamma consumes that budget in fewer rounds. This means the gamma=5/7/10 means are estimated from far fewer independent samples (~51-52 rounds) than gamma=1/3 (67-119 rounds), so the small dip from gamma=5 to gamma=10 (3.980 -> 3.904) should not be over-interpreted as a confirmed real effect -- it is plausibly within noise given the reduced sample size, though the overall rise-then-plateau shape is a robust, expected pattern.
p1_4_gamma_scan.cross_check_against_alpha: Under the simplifying assumption that each candidate is accepted independently with constant probability alpha (results/p1_0_gate_result.json overall_alpha = 0.7685), the expected round length as gamma -> infinity converges to 1/(1-alpha) ~= 4.32. All measured means (peak 3.980) stay below this theoretical ceiling with no violation, which is a good sanity check. Measured values also sit somewhat below what the constant-alpha formula would predict at each gamma (e.g. ~3.43 predicted vs 3.980 measured at gamma=5 by one directional comparison, ~4.08 predicted vs 3.904 measured at gamma=10) -- the direction of this gap is consistent with (but does not prove) the hypothesis that acceptance probability is not actually constant across positions within a round: later candidates in a long chain are drafted conditioned on the draft model's own earlier guesses rather than target-confirmed tokens, which could plausibly make deeper positions harder to accept than the average alpha suggests. Not investigated further in this pass.
p1_4_gamma_scan.practical_implication: For this draft/target pair, gamma=5 already captures nearly all of the achievable token-count benefit; gamma=7 and gamma=10 show no further token-count gain and, per the earlier wall-clock reasoning (draft_propose always drafts all gamma candidates sequentially regardless of where a rejection would occur), would spend more wasted sequential draft-model compute on average without any offsetting benefit. gamma=5 looks like a reasonable candidate 'sweet spot', but this is a token-count-only conclusion -- confirming it requires an actual wall-clock throughput measurement (the still-pending P4 task), not just this token-count curve.
p1_4_gamma_scan.overall_result: Descriptive/exploratory -- no pass/fail gate defined for this stage.
